title: Short Stuff: Mystery of the Sarah Jo
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1979 disappearance of the Sarah Jo, a 17-foot Boston Whaler that left Hana, Maui with five construction workers on a fishing trip and vanished. In September 1988, marine biologist John Naughton found the boat and a burial site on an uninhabited Marshall Islands atoll (Tamgi/Tamana area as spoken). Remains were identified by the US Army Central Identification Lab in Hawaii as Scott Mormon. Hosts discuss theories about how the boat drifted, how he died, and a possible Chinese fishing crew burial based on joss paper with foil lining, and the unanswered questions about the other four men.

segments.title: Opening banter and sources
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Short Stuff, thank Strange Company and the Maui Times and LA Times for research help, and joke about maritime disasters.

segments.title: The fishing trip and disappearance
segments.summary: Scott Mormon and four construction workers take the Sarah Jo, a 17-foot Boston Whaler borrowed from Robert Malayakini, on a fishing trip from Hana, Maui in 1979. Sea turns within two hours and a gale follows. Coast Guard searches about a week and friends and family search another month without finding anything.

segments.title: Boat and remains found in 1988
segments.summary: In September 1988, marine biologist John Naughton, who had been on the earlier search, spotted a Hawaiian-registered boat on an uninhabited Marshall Islands atoll. Nearby he found a burial mound with a driftwood cross, jawbone fragment, more skeletal remains, and a partly burned stack of paper.

segments.title: Open questions
segments.summary: Hosts list the unanswered questions: how the boat got so far, how and when the man died, who buried him, and where the other four men are.

segments.title: Identification and family theories
segments.summary: The US Army Central Identification Lab in Hawaii identified the remains as Scott Mormon but could not determine cause or time of death. The family thought he may have reached land alive and died of exposure, while others suggested he was strapped to the boat.

segments.title: Joss paper and Chinese fishermen burial theory
segments.summary: A stack of small foil-lined papers found at the site may be joss paper, used in Chinese funeral customs as spirit money. This suggests Chinese fishermen may have buried him, possibly within a six-year window. A 1982 survey of the atoll did not mention a boat, raising the question of whether it was missed or the boat arrived later.

segments.title: Drift speculation and illegal fishing
segments.summary: Hosts speculate about a three-year drift across the Pacific, possibly near Point Nemo, and say the burying crew may have been illegal fishermen who did not report the find but gave the remains a respectful burial.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up Short Stuff and the iHeartRadio production credit runs.
